statements.quote: Finally, they reflected on the value of collaborating with GenAI, detailing its tangible impacts on their creative work and sharing personal insights from their experiences (see Appendix B).
With participants’ consent, all interviews were audio-recorded, with each session lasting approximately 50 min on average. The recordings were transcribed into 139,000 words of textual data.
The main categories, subcategories, initial concepts, and illustrative quotes from Study 1 are presented in Appendix C (see Appendix C).

The creative task in Study 2a was adapted from Noy and Zhang (2023) (see Appendix D), and the descriptive materials for the idea generation and elaboration phases were drawn from Mannucci and Perry-Smith (2022) (see Appendix E).

The participants completed two product marketing-related creativity tasks in sequence (see Appendix D). A key distinction lay in task execution: in one task, participants collaborated with GenAI during the idea elaboration phase, whereas in the other, they worked independently (see Appendix F).

To standardize human–GenAI collaboration, we developed a custom online system that guided participants’ interactions with GenAI during specific creative phases (Chen & Chan, 2024). The system integrated a GenAI interface via an application programming interface (API—a software bridge that allows different systems to communicate and exchange data) to enable controlled collaboration, with technical support provided by professional software engineers.
The study was preregistered on AsPredicted (https://aspredicted.org/2hsq-9sg4.pdf).
The creative task in Study 3 was adapted from Chen and Chan (2024) (see Appendix G).

Consistent with Study 2, the materials for manipulating the human–GenAI collaboration phase were adapted from Mannucci and Perry-Smith (2022). The manipulation of perceived GenAI intelligence combined two approaches: a news-report method adapted from Yam et al. (2021) and a recall method from Maner et al. (2007) (see Appendix H). The former presented news excerpts describing GenAI intelligence levels, whereas the latter asked participants to recall and describe recent experiences of perceiving high or low GenAI intelligence, thereby enhancing the manipulation effect through the recall paradigm.
The specific measurement items used in this study are presented in Appendix I.

deposits.notes: The paper's p. 7, Section 6.1 link returns HTTP 200 HTML displaying preregistration #215503, 'Human-GAI collaboration and creativity', dated 2025-03-03. The page's Download PDF link was followed without authentication; it returned HTTP 200 application/pdf, a one-page file with Content-Disposition filename 'AsPredicted #215503.pdf' and 183429 bytes. The entire PDF was read in memory. It contains hypotheses, planned measures, four conditions, exclusions, and an approximate planned sample size, but no participant observations, realized assignments, outcome scores, participant proposals, analysis code, or dataset links. The anonymous author display is for blind review and does not restrict public reading. Q3 prespecifies novelty and usefulness assessed by three blinded marketing experts; it does not designate one outcome as primary. This supplies protocol information relevant to final.open_items item 6, not missing statistics. The flags describe actual participant data, not the presence of a description of experimental arms. No data-reuse license was stated in the inspected protocol.

Discovered in DataCite's first-author search: doi:10.17605/osf.io/pd9cf, 'The same knife cuts different bread: The different Benefits of GAI Use on Different phases of Creativity', registered 2024-07-16 by Shiyingzi Huang (OSF user r975k). The OSF user's verified ORCID 0009-0002-6417-5320 matches the paper's first-author ORCID link. The registration describes two within-person lab experiments, planned recruitment of 45 students per experiment, compensation of 40 RMB, GenAI during generation versus elaboration, and expert creativity ratings. These closely match S2 and S3 (paper Studies 2a and 2b), but the current title/DOI is not linked; studies_covered is therefore unclear rather than an asserted mapping. Public registration responses include manipulation instructions and an analysis plan, not data or code. https://api.osf.io/v2/registrations/pd9cf/ returned 200; has_data, has_analytic_code, has_materials, and has_supplements were false, all uploader arrays were empty, and no external URLs appeared in registration responses. https://api.osf.io/v2/nodes/pd9cf/files/osfstorage/ returned 200 with zero files. The files/provider endpoint https://api.osf.io/v2/registrations/pd9cf/files/ returned 200 and listed only the osfstorage folder, which is not counted as a file. The requested nodes/pd9cf/children/ endpoint returned 404 because this object is a registration; the correct https://api.osf.io/v2/registrations/pd9cf/children/ returned 200 with zero children. The registration resources endpoint returned 200 with zero linked resources. The license relationship https://api.osf.io/v2/licenses/563c1cf88c5e4a3877f9e96a/ returned 200 and identifies CC-By Attribution 4.0 International. The materials_only classification refers to instructions embedded in registration responses, despite the absence of uploaded material files. Its registered_from relationship points to the nonpublic source project fpjtg, recorded separately.

Source project identified by the public pd9cf registration's registered_from relationship, not by a data-sharing statement in the paper. The web URL returns HTTP 200 only for the generic OSF application shell. https://api.osf.io/v2/nodes/fpjtg/, https://api.osf.io/v2/nodes/fpjtg/files/osfstorage/, and https://api.osf.io/v2/nodes/fpjtg/children/ each returned HTTP 401 with 'Authentication credentials were not provided.' These read-only requests were issued together; no further access was attempted after the restriction was observed. No login, account creation, or access request was made. The private project's file count, contents, license, and correspondence to the published study data cannot be established. An account may also require project authorization; account_required records the observed authentication barrier, not a claim that simply registering would grant access. Empty files means no files could be listed, not a confirmed empty project.

notes: Checked 2026-10-09. Read the complete 122143-character markdown conversion, including Appendices A-I and references, and checked the quoted passages against PDF text using PyMuPDF. Quotes preserve the PDF wording; line wrapping and discretionary soft hyphens were normalized. The saved version is the 16-page journal article, International Journal of Information Management 86 (2026) 102986, available online 2025-10-03. No data/code availability statement, promise of data on request, or separate supplementary-file link appears in the paper; forms/c067.json data_and_code.data_url and code_url are empty. The paper includes interview respondent profiles and selected quotations for nonrandomized S1 plus experimental tasks, manipulation instructions, and scales. Those in-paper materials are not public randomized-study records. The only external protocol/data/materials link printed in the paper is the Study 3 AsPredicted protocol, which is public. The article DOI https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijinfomgt.2025.102986 returned HTTP 200 at https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0268401225001185, an HTML redirect page; the ScienceDirect landing page returned 403, so publisher supplements could not be verified. Title and first-author searches of DataCite, Zenodo, Harvard Dataverse, and OSF found no public participant dataset. The additional OSF registration found by author is a strong but unconfirmed match to the lab studies; its public file inventory is empty, and the linked source project requires authentication with unknown contents. Overall status describes the confirmed public content: protocols/materials only. It does not claim that the private project contains restricted participant data or that no unpublished/publicly unindexed deposit exists. No dataset rows or columns were available to inspect, so no missing statistic in final.open_items can be computed from confirmed public data: Study 3 exact cell counts and arm means/SDs/SEs (item 5), the perceived-intelligence-factor contrasts (item 8), and lab paired total-effect statistics (item 7) remain unavailable from participant records. Participant creative texts needed for diversity measures were not found. The public preregistration clarifies planned outcomes for item 6 but supplies no realized data. Confidence is medium because publisher supplements and private-project contents are inaccessible and the OSF-to-paper match is inferential. All online requests used Python urllib with User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1. The User-Agent contained no email address or personal identifier, and no credentials were sent. No downloaded files were saved.
